title: Encounters with the Curriculum
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans introduces a concept he calls Encounters with the Curriculum: the proportion of scheduled lesson time a pupil is actually in the lesson. He argues schools track attendance but rarely aggregate lessons missed, interruptions, removals and timeouts, so the true scale of lost learning is invisible. He sees the best schools raising time in lessons through attendance, behaviour and coping strategies, but treating them as separate efforts when the root causes are often shared. Grounding it as a social justice issue, he says a liberal curriculum should reach every child, not just an elite. He then critiques the IPPR 'lost learning' framing for treating all time out of class as exclusion, noting that some managed moves, internal exclusion or home education can be beneficial, and he calls for data that both quantifies and qualifies absence while weighing the individual against the cohort.
points: Schools usually know daily attendance but not what share of lesson time each pupil actually spends in lessons once truancy, removals and interruptions are added.
Attendance, behaviour, and intervention strategies are often run separately even though the reasons pupils miss lessons are frequently the same.
Evans frames access to a broad curriculum as social justice, joining a traditionalist stance with a commitment to inclusion.
Labelling all time out of class as 'exclusion' is pejorative and misses cases where moves or internal exclusion improve later access.
Any data collection must weigh teacher workload and the trade-offs between one child's access and the quality of experience for the rest.
quotes: I believe that this is a very important concept. I am going to call it Encounters with the Curriculum (EwtC, or yoot-see as I pronounce it in my head).
These interruptions are often unrecorded or inconsistently captured so that the problem may be recognised, but it cannot be fully measured or understood.

The reasons a pupil misses school, resists getting to the lesson on time, gets removed for their poor behaviour, drops a subject, is removed for intervention, or frequently ask to go to the medical room are often the same.

My ethical position is that such a curriculum should not be encountered only by the elite, but accessible to all. It is this set of values and beliefs that unites my fairly traditionalist stance on education with a commitment to inclusion.
We might characterise the opposed positions on this matter as those who believe exclusions are evil and those who believe they are a necessary evil.
As a headteacher, these trade offs were the substance of every day decisions. Few headteachers survive this experience with their idealism intact.
The key problem with this framing is that the term ‘exclusion’ is pejorative, yet some of the reasons listed should not necessarily attract our disapproval.
The call to address ‘lost learning’ is compelling, but rhetoric often masks nuance. We should also not underestimate the difficulty of collecting the data we need.
